Chapter 4: Making Tasks Manageable and Building Momentum.
Picture this: you’ve done the emotional prep work, but now you’re staring down a mountain of tasks that just seem... well, impossible to start. Sound familiar? Procrastination loves to show up when things feel too big, too vague, or just downright intimidating. When that happens, our minds start hunting for any excuse to escape, and the whole cycle of avoidance kicks right back in.
So, what can you do? Here’s a trick that really works—break those big tasks into smaller, bite-size pieces. Think of it like chopping a huge log into kindling. Suddenly, each piece feels lighter, doable, and a lot less scary. When you focus on just one small step, the overwhelm shrinks, and taking action gets so much easier.
There’s even a name for this: behavioral activation. The idea is simple but powerful—action comes before motivation. You don’t have to wait until you feel ready or inspired, because honestly, that moment might never come. Instead, just taking the tiniest step forward can spark a little momentum, and before you know it, you’re moving.
Let’s say you’ve got a huge writing project. Instead of trying to tackle the whole thing at once, you might just open a blank document and jot down a couple of quick ideas. That single act of starting—no matter how small—makes the work less intimidating and gives you a boost of confidence.
Here’s another thing that helps: focus on the process, not the outcome. Perfectionism loves to feed procrastination, because when you feel like you have to get everything just right, it’s tough to even begin. If you shift your attention to just doing the work, rather than worrying about the final result, the pressure melts away.
For example, if you’re a professional working on a report, try setting a timer for just ten minutes. Promise yourself you’ll work for those ten minutes—no matter what comes out. Forget about perfection. Just focus on making progress, not nailing it on the first try.
So, what are some practical ways to make big tasks feel smaller?
First, break large projects into specific, actionable steps.
Second, set a short timer and commit to working for that chunk of time.
And third, focus on simply getting started—don’t worry about finishing just yet.
When you make tasks feel more manageable, you cut down on that urge to avoid them. Every small step forward gives you a little win, and those wins add up, building a habit of action instead of avoidance.
